title: We Are Leaving Behind a Growing Number of Struggling Readers
author: Mark Schneider
summary: Mark Schneider argues that two decades of policy focus on proficiency under No Child Left Behind has obscured a growing group of students who score below NAEP Basic in reading. Nationally, the share of eighth graders below Basic has risen from about one fifth to one third over twelve years, meaning many cannot find the main idea or order of events in a text. He presents state-by-state data showing that even high performers such as Massachusetts leave a quarter of students below Basic, and that Mississippi's celebrated gains still leave over a third of eighth graders there. His proposed actions are to extend evidence-based reading instruction beyond the early grades, train middle school teachers to teach foundational reading, and build data systems that identify struggling readers year to year. He concludes that returning to NCLB's original promise means no longer overlooking the students furthest behind.
points: The share of U.S. eighth graders below NAEP Basic in reading has grown from about one fifth to one third over twelve years.
State league tables built on average scores hide large groups of students below Basic, even in high-performing states such as Massachusetts and New Jersey.
Science of Reading investment is concentrated in kindergarten through grade three, but the need is just as severe by eighth grade.
Many middle school teachers were trained to teach content, not to diagnose or remediate basic reading gaps, so they need training in evidence-based reading instruction.
States need data systems that track struggling readers every year rather than waiting for NAEP results every two years.
quotes: Perhaps the most undesirable side effect of the nation’s decades-long focus on student proficiency is that we have neglected the large and growing percentage of students who score below NAEP Basic in reading.
Simply put, about one-third of American eighth graders have trouble doing simple tasks such as identifying the order of events and finding the main idea in a text (See Figure 1).
Even as we celebrate the so-called Mississippi Miracle, over one third of Mississippi’s eighth graders are below NAEP Basic in reading.
Most reading investments and Science of Reading implementation are concentrated in kindergarten through third grade. But the data above shows the problem is just as severe by eighth grade.

Many middle school teachers were trained to teach content, not how to identify or remediate basic reading gaps. Closing this gap means giving them the same kind of training in evidence-based reading instruction that elementary teachers increasingly receive.

Right now, the country largely learns about this problem every two years, when NAEP results are released. States need stronger, better-connected data systems that let them identify struggling readers year to year, not waiting for the next national assessment

NCLB’s focus on proficiency was needed to pressure states and the nation to improve all students’ learning. But by focusing on proficiency, we’ve left too many children behind, as reflected in the growing percentages of those who score below NAEP Basic.
